core: Montage as a patterned juxtaposition or assembly of shots whose relation creates meaning
How contrast, repetition, sequence, duration, and rhythm can organize a montage pattern
A method for describing shot relations before making an interpretive claim
supporting: The French origin of the word and the historical importance of Soviet montage theory
The Kuleshov effect as a teaching concept about contextual meaning
Distinctions among montage, general editing, continuity editing, and parallel editing
outOfScope: A full history of Soviet cinema, detailed biographies, or study of a particular copyrighted sequence
Software workflows or a claim that montage determines a universal audience emotion
Treating every sequence of cuts as montage in the narrow analytic sense

claims.claim: Montage derives from a French word for assembly and can name a patterned arrangement of shots whose juxtaposition creates relations beyond any one image alone.
Soviet montage theorists and filmmakers of the 1920s gave special attention to how juxtaposed images could shape audience interpretation rather than simply preserve linear spatial continuity.
The Kuleshov effect is a teaching concept for the proposition that viewers can derive a different meaning from adjacent shots than from an isolated shot.
A montage pattern can use contrast, repetition, changes in duration, or shifts among images to organize comparison and rhythm.
Montage need not preserve stable geography or linear narrative progression in the way continuity editing often does.
Formal viewing can analyze montage by attending to length of shots, frequency of cuts, rhythm, continuity, and the relation of images to each other.
A responsible montage interpretation identifies the specific images and repeated relations, then states a qualified claim rather than assigning a fixed meaning or private intention.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No usable lesson, evidence packet, or source-linked four-option question set existed for this planned montage topic.
correctionsNeeded: Created a focused montage lesson that distinguishes patterned juxtaposition from the broader work of editing and from continuity-oriented cutting.
Used hypothetical sequences rather than reproducing or closely analyzing film clips, screenshots, or dialogue.
Added five source-linked four-option questions with verified answer keys and no positional skew.
